en: Preface to the *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra):
Śākyamuni Buddha employed his lips and tongue for forty-nine years, speaking at length both horizontally and vertically, and expounding both openly and secretly.
A hundred methods are all snares for deceiving people; a thousand kinds of hammers and tongs are nothing but the tradition of forging steel.
They cause one to choke on them within the breast, unable to vomit them out, such that they all become both medicine and disease.
If one possesses superior faculties and sharp wisdom, one must tear asunder these snares and smash through this mass of doubt, [realizing] each and every thing from within one's own breast.

It flows forth; one discards the old and opens the new. It begins with covering heaven and earth. Generally speaking, when studying the teachings, one must attain genuine practice that reaches the ultimate goal;
only then will there be true realization and benefit. One must investigate authentically and awaken authentically.

Regarding the words of the *patriarchal vehicle* and the scriptures, one must certainly grasp the true intent of the Tathāgata; do not cling to the literal text to interpret the meaning, nor give rise to conceptual understanding based on mere words.
Directly penetrating the essential meaning, one accords with and realizes the original mind. Unlearned wisdom manifests before one; the Way of innate truth is no longer obscured.
All is resolved within oneself, merging in silent harmony without omission. Thus, not even a hair’s breadth of the appearance of written words is perceived.

As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Upon hearing the teaching of the Great Nirvāṇa, do not conceive the notion of 'words' regarding a single character or a single phrase, nor conceive the notion of 'phrases'."
One does not construct the marks of letters, nor the marks of the Buddha, nor the marks of preaching. Such a meaning is called the "mark of no-marks.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the Tathāgata’s wondrous eloquence, both vertical and horizontal, which breathes forth and swallows empty space;

the sharp edge beneath his tongue performs miraculous transformations, continuous and dense like an echo in a valley. Its entire substance is the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama; its entire substance is...
It flows forth from the great ocean of quiescent extinction, vast and expansive. Its language is挥洒 (huīshā)—a free and unrestrained expression—like a cascading torrent.

With its sharp points buried and its brilliance sheathed, it becomes ever more wondrous with every transformation; one cannot fathom its depth. It blends the mind and blends all views, leaving those who are deluded in a state of bewilderment.
In this state, the mind has no realm of right or wrong, and views have no domain of right or wrong. Upon encountering any object, it is immediately the mind; thus, right and wrong [are transcended].

It is the simultaneous forgetting of both. From within this true, essential, wondrously enlightened, and luminous nature, there has thus emerged the Great Capacity and Great Function of the Tathāgata.
He secretly manifested traces through provisional means, and the Most Holy One bestowed his signs; how could this be without purpose?

Therefore, by thoroughly exhausting the subtle essence, one attunes the words and penetrates the fundamental doctrine; by harmonizing with the fundamental doctrine, one suddenly clarifies the mind and its perceptions. This is the single flavor—
Gao: When the river is divided, he rises briefly; seeing no manifold directions, his mind has no deviant paths.

He constantly contemplates the subtle and wondrous eloquence of the Tathāgata, manifesting the true mind within words and revealing the true mind through responding to conditions, demonstrating the true mind through direct speech.

All these are the manifestations of the Tathāgata’s awakened mind: the methods of vocal transformation, the subtleties of literary inspiration, and the expansion of the mind that equalizes self and others.

Realizing that verbal expressions are not the ultimate reality, then even though one responds to ten thousand changes and engages in a thousand distinct actions of speech and movement, all remain within the Tathāgata’s own abiding samādhi.
The profound mystery of a single sūtra can thus be understood through this single principle.

Thus, nothing is left out. Therefore, when the mind perceives things as merging into one, it is like adding feet to a snake’s body. By analyzing the root and analyzing the objects of perception, both subject and object are forgotten.

Yet those who dwell in dull emptiness and vacuous stillness cannot adapt to circumstances or capacities to scrutinize the Tathāgata’s wondrous eloquence, thereby failing to realize their inherently unmoving mind.
They empty themselves of intellectual understanding and sweep away all views and hearing, eradicating emotional consciousness.

Thus, delusive thoughts are severed; the celestial faculty is triggered, and all myriad concerns become empty. He manifests the marvels of granting and revoking, and practices the subtleties of killing and enlivening.

This singular, transformative wonder is like the rain sent by dragons and spirits. Therefore, though one exhausts their wisdom and deliberation, and tires their physical strength, they cannot fathom his vision;
though they search the profound pivot and reach the limits of the Dharma-treasury, they cannot complete his exposition. To analyze...
The "neighboring atom" (paramāṇu) initiates the refinement of vision, yet one cannot exhaustively grasp its mind. Now, the Word is but one; it is uniquely manifest, a浑然 (hún-rán) single entity.
When encountering objects, the mind merges with them, like a pearl rolling upon a tray—circulating everywhere without obstruction.

As it harmonizes with sounds and is revealed, whether grasped horizontally or inverted, all these are expressions of the mind. How could one possibly seek it word by word or assemble it phrase by phrase?
Thus, as they followed the wind to catch the echoes, their doubts and obstructions were suddenly cleared away, and they were no longer hindered by mere words and letters.
Yet those who merely cling to and recite these teachings daily fall into fragmentation, lacking any ground of true realization;

they give rise to root-delusions and doubts, like mistaking a foul-smelling object for sandalwood or taking up tiles and rubble for refined gold. For this reason, the lofty and wise knit their brows, beating their breasts in deep anguish.
Regarding chronic and terminal illnesses that reach the vital points of the body, even the divine physician folds his hands and looks on from the sidelines.
Yet, if one realizes this through personal experience, it manifests entirely within the daily lives of ordinary people. Therefore, if one's practice is not dedicated, one cannot attain awakening;

if the mind does not awaken, it cannot bring about transformation; if awakening is not authentic, it cannot lead to penetration; and if vision is not awakened, it cannot achieve integration. Thus, one must exhaustively investigate these transformations.
Transformed by a thousand words, he reveals the single mind within the myriad dharmas; his eloquence becomes increasingly refined, and the more it is exhausted, the more wondrous it becomes.
All of this is the divine function of the post-enlightenment effort—most easy and most simple, a void-perfect and wondrous responsiveness.
*The Illumination of Key Passages of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, composed by Dàsháo.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness... [until] ...they returned to the presence of the Buddha.
When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he first manifests the true essence and emits radiance; transformation Buddhas sit cross-legged upon his tongue,
emitting divine light as they proclaim incantations to reveal inconceivable spiritual transformations that cannot be reached by consciousness or attained through discursive thought.

When Ānanda saw the Buddha, he prostrated himself in worship and wept with grief, lamenting that from time immemorial he had not witnessed such great strategic maneuvers, great eloquence, great mechanisms, and great functions of the Tathāgata.

He thought that these must surely have originated from a fundamental source, manifesting infinite transformations and marvelous displays of both granting and withholding, thereby fully expressing the Buddha’s original intent. There was nothing that did not...
From the initial arousal of a single thought, one swallows and spits out the Yangtze River; its surging currents and hanging waterfalls are the natural operation of the vital breath.
One must, within the written words, manifest the Tathāgata’s Dharma-eye, its radiance pervading all places, such that every utterance contains gold and spews forth jade.
One must recognize the true substance of this jade; thus, whether speaking freely or setting pen to paper, there is nothing that does not penetrate its subtle essence.
Generally speaking, when one speaks without recognizing its master, how can one know that which first attains the ultimate rectitude within the mind?

Only that which has attained the ultimate rectitude within the mind may be extended to all under heaven and shared with them. When the mind has not yet moved, it is difficult to recognize it in its true state;
once it moves, its spiritual transformations are unfathomable, and as it transforms, its expressions become indeterminate. How, then, could one recognize its master? It is the True Master.
I do not yet understand. How could one possibly discern the mind or its characteristics within words, as if attempting to distinguish milk within water?

Thus, as soon as a thought arises, its brilliant colors manifest and its vital structure is fully revealed—like a soaring dragon shaking the sea, with clouds and mists arising from all four directions.
Seizing the moment and responding to conditions, it undergoes a thousand transformations; where might its spirit not go? As for its speech...
What is not swift? It does not emerge from within the flow of conceptual thought, yet it manifests great capacity and great function.
All arise from the source of a single thought-moment; extending to a thousand or ten thousand thoughts, they constitute the wondrous purport that threads them together.
This can hardly be produced through deliberation or conjecture; one must tread upon the ground of reality itself. And so it is...
Unsettled thoughts arise; unsettled words flow forth; unsettled traces manifest. Thus, the true countenance of the Tathāgata is revealed.
The heart-light of all Buddhas is likewise so. Sentient beings have, from the beginning, no two distinct natures.
For this reason, Ānanda made his request: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained the wondrous Bodhi..."
Śamatha and samādhi are the essential means for the initial stage and the source of their arousal. Thus the World-Honored One asked:

"When you first resolved your mind, what superior sign did you perceive within my Dharma? Therefore, in debating the fundamental tenets of the Tathāgata, one must recognize the underlying purport of the Dharma;
only then can the faculty of the student and the teaching of the teacher strike in resonance. And so, one must recognize...
Only when one understands the question can one know that the answer is without error.

Therefore, as soon as Ānanda saw the Tathāgata open his mouth and move his tongue, he asked what superior marks he perceived within the Dharma; Ānanda immediately replied, "I see the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, which are supremely wondrous and extraordinary;
his physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli, and is not produced by the craving of desire."

The World-Honored One further said: "You should all know that all sentient beings fail to realize that this is the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. Look at these two [views]: one points to it as the thirty-two marks."
One may point to it as the "ever-abiding true mind," yet little do they realize that these are all the various transformations and radiant light emitted from the tip of the Tathāgata’s tongue;
therein, the true essence and its manifestations are mutually fused, nature and appearance are equal, and the provisional and the ultimate are practiced in tandem.
Simultaneous like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a hen and her chick, the sharp edge of the wind is revealed; the lineage of discourse is a single thread.
Can you yet discern whether this is form, or mind, or the attainment of Bodhi? Is it the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna?
The Tathāgata’s miraculous power is not merely marvelous in its capacity for transformation;
one must know that the unchanging true body all issues from the single thought of the true source.

Thus it manifests as samādhi and dhyāna, or as the thirty-two marks, or as the permanently abiding true mind—it is precisely this that constitutes the three transformations described in the text. Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

I command you to respond with a straightforward mind; you must know that the true essence of the Dharma lineage is like a *karkarava* horn pillow—its patterns manifest according to conditions, yet it immediately ascends to the realm of the divine and subtle to respond to myriad occasions.

It can cause one to be carefree within this state, directly reaching the Tathāgata’s ground of reality, and can meet the sharp blades of incoming stimuli. This may truly be called the ultimate [teaching] of the World-Honored One.
To see through to the very bottom is nothing other than following this single thought, this drop of vital bloodline.
When spirit merges and bones are saturated, there is nothing hidden that does not manifest, and nothing subtle that does not become apparent; thus it serves as the primary expedient.
Therefore, with a single drop of water, one can stir the long river into curds and milk, attaining joy for oneself and bestowing joy upon others.
Then the Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said, it is truly what one loves and delights in... [it] actually dwells within the body.
In examining the Dharma of the Tathāgata, one must not merely fixate on the literal words or engage in speculative interpretation. The Tathāgata...
This is what is truly alive and active. [The Buddha] asked Ānanda: "When you first resolved to attain enlightenment, with the thirty-two marks as your object, what was it that you saw?
Who was it that felt this love and delight? Ānanda replied: "It was by means of my mind and eyes that I felt such love and delight. The Buddha said:
"As you have said, it is indeed because of the mind and eyes that one feels true love and delight. If one does not recognize the mind and eyes..."
Wherever one may be, if one cannot subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), the Tathāgata’s adornment is most extraordinary and his application of the Dharma is most profound.
Therefore, he first pierced a single aperture at the crown of the head and emitted radiance, causing all sentient beings to clearly perceive their own true faces.
Thus it is said: "It is just as you have said. This single word "said" (*shuo*) is the thief's—
It is attained here and now. It is seen in the very place where mind and eye reside. The thirty-two marks are manifest.
Thus, one may see that the Tathāgata does not emerge from the flow of deliberation or conjecture; yet he expounds the entire Great Canon without expending even the slightest effort.

The mere word "only" exhausts the undertakings of a thousand ages. This spoken character is precisely the locus of the Tathāgata’s great eloquence, the locus of the great pivot, the locus of the great function, and the locus of great meditative concentration.

It is the place where all Buddhas are born, the place where the Dharma-body of the Buddhas of the ten directions is revealed, and the place where the original face of all sentient beings is seen. It penetrates through to the very core.
It passes through the channels and blood-vessels and reveals the traces of true seeing; therefore, it does not abide within the body, nor is it internal, external, or in between.
Thus, it is free from the delusions of consciousness, mind, discrimination, and conceptual signs.
This is the true nature of all Buddhas and the fundamental source of all sentient beings; it is the primordial, pure essence of Nirvana—pure, wondrously pure.
This is that which clarifies the mind. When sentient beings awaken to this, they recognize their own face prior to the empty kalpa;
the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise all thus. Therefore, there is no entanglement in the slightest, and there is not a single trace of a conceptual framework.
If a student merely follows the words and pursues the literal meaning, they will be lost regarding the true eye. Ānanda was indeed quite clever; he immediately said:
The blue lotus eyes are likewise upon the Buddha’s face, yet the ten kinds of ordinary beings all take their consciousness and mind to reside within the body.
The floating faculties and the four sense-objects are merely on my face. One might say, Ānanda, that you have identified the source of both the true and the false with extreme clarity.
Only by doing so can one follow the current upstream and directly sail across the Tathāgata’s great ocean of nirvāṇa. Thus it passes.
The critical juncture of the "Seven Investigations and Eight Returns" does not lie in hooked chapters or thorny sentences; how could the display of verbal sharpness compare?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall... (up to) "...you are able to see far off."
Śākyamuni has fully realized his original intent. The scale and mirror hang suspended; wind and thunder are held in his grasp.

Containing the great void within his breast, he manifests his own true face through all manner of transverse and vertical, inverted and upright, marvelous, orthodox, and strange expressions, so that all sentient beings may verify it for themselves.
Do you recognize where it is? Can you see the face of the Tathāgata?

Therefore it is said, "A straightforward mind answers me. Because the mind and its words are straightforward, from the beginning stages of the path to the final stage of realization, the Elder Śākyamuni did not need to deliberate or hesitate before speaking forth.
This is simply because when one reaches the point where the mind and its words are straightforward, one no longer recognizes the true face of the mind and its words;
they all emerge from the ground of ultimate reality. At the very moment a single thought arises...
It is so. Without the slightest pretense, it encompasses the most profound mysteries without omission and adapts to circumstances with inexhaustible flexibility.

It never alters its true countenance; yet, if the mind has not truly reached this state, then it manifests as wind-blown and thunder-clashed, vigorous and stirring, with spiritual transformations that are never fixed.
In a mere instant or a subtle moment, the World-Honored One now asks: "Within your hall now..."
"What did you see first? Ānanda replied, "I was in the hall; I saw the Tathāgata first.
Ultimately, one must recognize where Ānanda was when he was able to see the Tathāgata—it certainly was not within the realm of physical features or appearances.
Seizing this tongue that pursues the wind and chases the lightning, I shall point out the eye of the Tathāgata, so that you may see him directly.
The manifestation of the Tathāgata’s countenance flying through the void—how could it be sought within the visual perceptions of the eyes?
One might say that Ānanda was truly clever; he personally encountered that which is appropriate, for it is indeed the Tathāgata.
Who among those who observe the signs of the world does not compete to identify with them? Therefore, together with all [beings]...
All sentient beings are equal. Every single being fully manifests the marks of all Buddhas.
If a student merely follows the literal text and pursues the meaning, failing to recognize the true face of the Tathāgata, they will likewise be unable to recognize their own true face.
They will still harbor doubts regarding fundamental views within their chests, having not yet attained the state where mind and words cease.
The divine transformation within the state of directness has long been missed. One cannot fully perceive it with the eye of a Tathāgata.
As for the continuity of the lifeblood in the Tathāgata’s functioning—like drawing silk from a single cocoon—it reaches the very bottom in one thread, without interruption or obstruction.
This secret pivot of the Tathāgata will never be broken open for people; you must...
Only when one attains true realization and personally penetrates this pivotal point can one overturn the entire Great Canon of the Tathāgata, bringing it all into one’s own shell;
only then will one recognize the Tathāgata’s heroic ambition throughout the ages.
The true meaning was transmitted in several hundred thousand words, yet not a single superfluous word ever came forth.
This must have been achieved by a person of true caliber.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm amidst the great assembly... [up to] ...it would be impossible for such a thing to occur.

The nature has no function that it does not employ; when it employs them, they are immediately perceived. At present, those who speak of this nature are many, but those who realize its nature are few.
To realize it is necessarily to be able to see it truly; to see it is necessarily to know its own employment.

Through such employment, one then knows one's own mind, without depending on the power of another. Therefore, there is the distinction between the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body, for body and mind are not the same.
The function [of this]. The preceding passage revealed the essence of wisdom; this passage alone reveals the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Transmitting radiance and pouring forth fluidity, it does not depart from the boundaries of the compass and square. Observing capacities and adapting to tasks, it recognizes forms beyond the mundane.
When the Tathāgata tames lions and guides elephants, responding to norms and entering the compass, there is a distinct, singular flavor. Do you still recognize where the Tathāgata resides?
"Where did you see me? Ānanda had just seen the Tathāgata when the Buddha extended his arm and rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head, saying:
"To say that one was in the hall and could not see the Tathāgata, yet could see the groves and springs—such a thing is impossible. Formerly, Cui Yuan served as the Governor of Beiji.
Shan Zhang excelled at cursive script (*caoshū*). His graceful style surpassed others; his strokes were refined and subtle, and his spiritual transformations were unimpeded.
Like gold tempered a hundred times or the natural beauty of fine jade, he may truly be said to be "colder than ice, more clear than water."
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have heard that for the Tathāgata, there is no mental activity that is not purposeful, and there is no sphere of activity that is not the mind itself. When active, the mind can perceive its own characteristics;
when inactive, it cannot perceive the movement of its form. Whenever the mind is stirred, the body moves along with it. Thereupon [he ceased speaking].
There is an unmoving mind, yet the mind has no characteristic of movement. Ānanda, it is like the light of a lamp illuminating the space outside;
when the World-Honored One went to the Jīvaka Grove to take his midday meal, this was the manifestation of the characteristic of external movement.
Among all the hearts revealed in the world, there are none that do not rely upon food and drink; thus, the daily activities of the mind are stirred by them.
That the movement of food and drink is employed within the mind is true for every person alike. Is it not the case that when one person eats, [the effect is shared]?
The assembly all agreed with this. Therefore, they returned to the forest to observe the fast together, and in that same place, their physical forms were manifested.

There are four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*): first, gross material food and subtle food; second, nutriment by contact (*sparśa-āhāra*); third, nutriment by mental volition (*manas-karma-āhāra*); and fourth, nutriment by consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*).
The people of Jambudvīpa take flour, rice, and putrid meat as gross material food, while massage, bathing, and the application of ointments constitute subtle food.
"Subtle food.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, it is because one does not see within" (Chapter One).
One must by no means consider Ānanda to be someone who has not yet entered the Path; look, not a single word was spoken in vain.
Half-hidden and half-revealed, the mind and the faculty of sight both manifest in darkness. Ānanda said:
"This cognizant mind, being unable to know what is within yet able to see what is without—according to my reflection—it must be hidden within the faculties.
If one takes a crystal bowl and covers both eyes, that faculty continues to see and immediately makes distinctions; its inability to see what is within must mean it resides [there]."

Because it is the faculty (*indriya*), it gazes clearly at external objects; because there is no obstruction, it is hidden within the faculty. Ānanda, you have merely spoken of that which is "within the faculty":
is this the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)? Or is it the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-indriya*)?
That which follows the seeing—is it not the eye-faculty? That which immediately performs discrimination—is it not the tongue-faculty? Furthermore, he said: "That which does not see internally..."
Because it resides within the sense organ; does this not refer to the tongue-organ? Furthermore, as for the statement that one clearly gazes outward without obstruction, this is not the eye-organ.
Thus, regarding the locations of the mind and eyes as debated by Ānanda, there has not been a single word of error.
The Buddha said that such a person should have their eyes covered with a crystal cage; they would then see mountains and rivers, and see the crystal itself.
"No. Ānanda said, "I truly see the lapis lazuli. [The Master replied,] "This is not seeing with the eyes;
originally there is no difference. World-Honored One, you have clearly opened up my mind. If it were joined with the lapis lazuli, would you now be able to point it out and extract it?
His verbal prowess was brilliant and radiant; one could not measure the splendor of his eloquent words. It was not... [incomplete].
"Is it the tongue-faculty that, in accordance with what is seen and in accordance with what is discriminated [perceives]?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, I now further reflect in this way. (Chapter One)

Ānanda also used the transformation of written characters to reveal the location of the mind and the eyes; thus he said: "The internal organs (fu-zang) are within, while the apertures (qiao-xue) reside without.
Where there are organs, there is darkness; where there are apertures, there is light. These apertures do not refer merely to the opening of the mouth.
Therefore, when the mind is exposed, it is bright. Furthermore, it is said that opening the eyes to see light is called "seeing the external."
When closing the eyes and seeing darkness, this is called "seeing within. This refers to the location of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). The Tathāgata said:
"If you see light when opening your eyes, why do you not see your own face? If seeing your face were established, then this cognizing mind and the visual faculty [would both be seen]."
"It must be within empty space. If it were within empty space, then the Tathāgata would now see your face;
that would also be your own body. This Ānanda sees for himself, word for word, without depending on another. Therefore, when opening his eyes he sees light—why does he not see his own face?
Thus, as the Tathāgata has spoken, every word reveals that it is all empty space. Now..."
To see your face is also to see your body. If you maintain that there are two distinct perceptions for the body and the eyes, how could there be two separate cognitions?
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly that [all things] arise from the mind. (Chapter One)
Gathering the essence from the garden of literature and inhaling the *campaka* flowers of the Great Meaning, it follows that when the mind arises, phenomena manifest.
Now, examine this: which phrase is the arising mind? Which phrase is the manifesting phenomenon?
Which phrase is not the mind? Which phrase is not the phenomenon? Seeing that which is not the produced mind, the mind is not...
One sees with the eye, yet it is the eye that truly sees. When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise accordingly;
how could this depend on the substance of thought? Rather, wherever they conjoin—whether internally, externally, or in between—it is within these nineteen realms and seven objects that they meet.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have also heard that the Buddha and Mañjuśrī and others—Ānanda himself being constantly present among them, moving with such vitality as a pearl rolling upon a tray or a tray rolling over a pearl—as these various Dharma-Princes discourse on the true nature (*dharmatā*), the World-Honored One has also said it is neither within, nor without, nor in between. Since they speak thus...
Regarding the time of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): what dharma is this "true mark" that you speak of as internal, external, and intermediate?

Since there is nothing seen internally and no cognition externally, how could there be anything in between? If it is not fixed in its manifestation, how could one differentiate it within visual consciousness?
And how could it be both at once?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I have previously seen the Buddha together with Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
When an object exists, the mind exists; the mind does not cling to objects, yet both mind and object are established.
How could it be that when an object exists, the mind is absent? How could there be an object without a mind? If an object were without a mind, how could it fly through water or over land?”
...proceeding.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
As for the icchantika, it is because they lack the faculty of faith and so forth. *Mleccha*—here translated as "borderland"—is indeed [the term for] *icchantika*.
This refers to the place where retribution is received. To be able to attain *śamatha* is precisely to destroy the ground of retribution.
"Emitting various jewel-lights from the face-gate" represents the light emitted from the gate of the mouth;

this is the fundamentally pure essence of *nirvāṇa*, which is devoid of the marks of consciousness, thought, or perception, does not abide within the body, and is not subject to the subtle essence of consciousness that gives rise to all [phenomena].

This is the condition. One who does not lose the essence of original luminosity merely awakens to the fact that the words spoken from the mouth are themselves the true body of nirvana—without consciousness and without thought. Therefore, there is no deluded mind to engage in discrimination.

If even a hair’s breadth of the subtle essence of consciousness were to stir, then the entire body of original luminosity would become entirely deluded; thus, one would be bewildered by delusion throughout the entire day.
Having lost the essence of the original luminosity, they enter the various realms of existence in vain, remaining unaware of it themselves.

When the Tathāgata raised his arm and bent his fingers to demonstrate their true nature, Ānanda sought to investigate and pursue it through reasoning; therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked him, saying, "This is not your mind."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha;

because my heart loves the Buddha, (Chapter One), my mental consciousness shifts and transforms, its principles being without constancy. Understanding and delusion alternate with one another. To clarify the spirit and allow it to shine in emptiness, when a single thought moves, do not employ the consciousness.
Because its use has been habitual since beginningless time, at the moment of discerning through *vitarka* and *vicāra*, do not employ it."

Consciousness operates amidst forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, responding to stimuli like an echo; it is like the wind in a valley following the roar of a tiger, or auspicious clouds pursuing a soaring dragon.
Even if one maintains an inner state of profound stillness, this remains a mere reflection of the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmas*).
These two obstacles are not the true mind. If the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind were like empty space, then—
Discriminating between vitarka and vicāra constitutes the nature of conceptualization; this is truly your own mind.

For nine successive lifetimes you failed to attain the fruits of sainthood because, through deluded conceptualization, you had not yet awakened to true samādhi. Formerly, Yu Xin loved only the stele of Hanshan Temple.
When someone asked him about the North, Xin replied, "Only a single stone at Hanshan Temple is worthy of conversation."
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with profound sorrow and prostrated himself, casting his body to the ground.
To console Ānanda, the Tathāgata emitted from his breast a light that resembled many metaphors.
Therefore, true seeing does not rely on the eyes; the blind are not without mind. Just as a lamp’s light can reveal forms, it is like opening a path.
The light of the eye; it is taught as the sole nourishment that can satiate one with the flavor of the Dharma.
Like a son receiving [a treasure] from his father, all [these teachings] surge forth from the breast and bestow upon me samādhi.

Although Ānanda heard these words along with the great assembly, the World-Honored One is like a great smelter’s red furnace, refining sentient beings through a hundredfold trials. Those among sentient beings who do not undergo such refinement are truly sentient beings;
this is what Dharmapāla realized: that adventitious defilements are like travelers at an inn, while space is tranquil and still.
However, when the Tathāgata opens and closes his eyes, extends and clenches his fists, or radiates light to the left and right, these are manifestations of the Dharma-body;
there is not a single sign of movement. Since every thought-moment arises and perishes, how could there be a mind that is unmoving?

If one were to move, how could this be considered the true realm? How could empty space ever be said to be silent? Even if the head moves and shakes, the mind neither expands nor contracts; how could it ever be lost or forgotten?
And yet, do they act in a perverted manner? (Volume One, Qi).
The preceding seven inquiries regarding the text have been manifested three times. The first is called "emitting a hundred jewel-lights from the crown of the head";
the second is "the light emitted from the mouth"; the third is "the jewel-light surging forth from the chest. All of these are not separate from the Tathāgata.
It comes to the tip of the tongue and emits every word; all these are the light of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark, causing all sentient beings to verify it for themselves.
Furthermore, it cites the analogy of seeing a river to explain that the nature of the faculty’s vision is neither born nor extinguished, like a second moon.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"Fuxi drew the Eight Trigrams to manifest their forms; Xuanyuan brought forth the numinous tortoise to reveal its colors.
The *Yijing* says, 'The many dragons having no head brings good fortune. That Cook Ding could not see the ox as a whole was due to the Tathāgata’s golden-armed mark."
The inversion regarding the *tūla* cotton of the wheel [of saṃsāra]: all people neglect the place where the Dharma-body manifests.

Therefore, the various conditions of form and mind, and all dharmas that serve as objects, are merely manifestations of the mind alone. Yet, the sound of the ocean tide that arises is entirely a manifested mark of the wondrously luminous, true essence.
How could it be produced by the darkness and obscurity of emptiness? [It is not so for] your body or your mind.
It is the same single void. Just as the external mountains, rivers, void, and great earth are all this wondrously luminous true mind, unmixed with delusive thoughts—how could it ever be obscured?
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms [until the Buddha said]:
“I shall proclaim it for you: the mind does not arise without an object; phenomena do not arise without the mind. The mind arises following objects; phenomena arise pursuing conditions.
Phenomena have conditions, and the mind likewise has conditions. One points to the finger to see the moon; one follows the sound to find the mind. Sound is like...”
The guest pavilion is perceived by the mind through discrimination. The mind is like a reflected image based on conditions; phenomena likewise arise from conditions.
One must not seek the mind apart from discrimination, nor should one maintain that discrimination is utterly non-existent and thus obscure it as a dark, ultimate principle (*tattva*).
The perfect sound realized by Ānanda constitutes the perfection of the mind-ground.
The Tathāgata takes discernment as the mind to demonstrate the illusory nature of the true application of dharmas; one must know that speech is the true mind.
Now I shall demonstrate the ground of non-retrogression (until it is called "worthy of compassion").
The Tathāgata takes up the single character "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) as if it were a single blade of the Vajra King sword;

it can sever all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and can cut off both views and the conditions for views, opening up the opposition between roots and objects and sweeping away both the internal and external.
Only by severing all intermediate deliberations and conceptual calculations can one sharpen the edge of the divine sword;
one must examine things to attain knowledge. It was not anticipated that the Tathāgata would have so many discursive states within his breast to be embellished upon his tongue.
Its brilliant colors are revealed, so that when people behold it, they do not depart from the natural splendor of their original ground.

As it is spread forth and brought out, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east; as the sun rises in the heavens, there is radiant brilliance, along with all manner of transformative manifestations.
The wind in his throat suddenly shifted; the preceding realm became entirely empty.

A solitary peak stood alone in its emerald green, and only the Tathāgata’s wind-bone (spiritual frame) was seen, drifting serenely amidst the vast, azure mists like a dragonfly skimming the water—untouched by any worldly defilement.
"Ānanda, although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place of return... [until] who would be the objective phenomena?
Ānanda has already perfected the eye of wisdom and sees up to the first dhyāna; Aniruddha has already perfected the divine eye; the various bodhisattvas have clarified the Buddha-eye;
yet sentient beings possess only the fleshly eye. Thus, since the Dharma-eye is not yet perfected, it is difficult to find."
The nature within these words is precisely what the Tathāgata has now arrayed as objects within his speech:

the palaces of the sun and moon, the mountains of the seven precious metals, the rising clouds and flying birds, the moving winds and stirring dust, the grasses, trees, humans, and animals—all these are things that are not you.
Can you now further analyze them: who is the essence of "I," and what constitutes the objective phenomena? For whom have these objects been arrayed?
"What thing is this? it asks. "Who is the master within this realm? Who is the 'self' amidst these objective forms?
Is there anyone capable of depicting this scene and analyzing it so as to distinguish between the nostrils of Śākyamuni and Ānanda?
Who is the self? Who is the other? When object and realm laugh together, and person and image converse as one."
It is like a person from Yangzhou speaking with another; their accent and manner immediately reveal themselves. Luoshan said:

"In general, when preaching the Dharma, one must understand the life-and-death and killing-and-enlivening that occur right before one's eyes, and recognize the true master within words. Only then can one praise the sword that kills and the sword that enlivens.
One must grasp the critical pivot of the ancients and discern the true face of people today."
Ānanda, exhaustively trace the source of your vision from the palaces of the sun and moon until you truly realize the nature of your seeing.
The Tathāgata speaks of this with great fervor and will not let it rest; there are no such myriad images within my breast.
They all manifest their brilliance upon the tip of my tongue, leaving one with no ground upon which to observe them and no form by which to depict them—truly non-existent.

Within the realm of forms, their true nature is revealed: clouds rising and birds flying, winds stirring and dust rising, trees, mountains, rivers, and all categories of grasses, shrubs, humans, and animals—all are what Ānanda’s seeing-essence perceives.
This is precisely what those who study the Buddha today experience as well.
We shall now debate various matters. What is the nature of these objects? And what is it that corresponds to your "essence of seeing"?
If this seeing were an object, then you would likewise be able to see my seeing; if it were the same as seeing, it would be called "seeing me."
(He came to) seek the truth from me.
Opening his mind, he pursued the inquiry with intensity. The Tathāgata suddenly manifested transformations and wonders, emitting stones and holding gold.

He lightly moved the tongue of his sharp lips, chasing the wind and pursuing lightning as he produced a continuous stream of new sounds; yet these were certainly not to be judged by the color of a horse—whether it be a mare, a stallion, a black, or a yellow.

In the midst of this, where sound responds to resonance and kindred spirits seek one another, it is like the presence of red and purple among the five colors, or Zheng and Wei among the eight musical notes.

When depicting figures and recording sounds and rhythms, the crane and the snow must be distinguished. One describes the grand rhetoric that cannot be seen and discerns the realization within the sounds;
yet, though the soaring clouds are not seen, the brilliance of the literary blade shines forth. If one perceives them as being identical, this is called "seeing."
"This is the essence of seeing. If you can see my seeing, then it is not the case that only material objects can be seen.
Once the essence of the faculty of seeing is clearly understood, it must not be confused with the state of non-seeing.
If seeing were a material object, then you could indeed see my seeing; yet when I am not seeing, why do you not see me?"
This place where nothing is seen cannot be compared to the essence of seeing.

It is the ground of non-seeing that the Tathāgata has brought forth from his mouth and presented for all people to seek and see. Thus, while the Tathāgata can see what is not seen within his own mouth, layer upon layer of seeing is spread out;
therefore, when the Tathāgata demonstrates this state of non-seeing, all people are unable to perceive it.
Yet there is no person who can see it. How could there not be a place that is not seen? Thus, there is the capacity to see through seeing, rather than the capacity to see through non-seeing.
If one can see within the realm of non-seeing, then one knows that the seeing of the "capacity to see" is not true seeing;
it is the seeing of non-seeing that constitutes true seeing. If it is the seeing of non-seeing, and...
One is able to see it. It is naturally not that state of non-seeing; yet, does one still see it?
For this reason, the ground of non-seeing is revealed, and one discriminates between the marks of seeing and non-seeing, while failing to see that discrimination within seeing.
What is it that sees together with it? Who is it that does not see? How can it be said thus?
"It is not seen. Yet who is it that sees? One is able to distinguish between the characteristics of seeing and not seeing.
Since you say we see the same thing, yet you cannot distinguish the characteristic of seeing, it is said: 'If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing.'"
This spontaneity is not something that objects can see. Ānanda did not realize the seeing of the capacity to see, yet he sought it within the ground where the Tathāgata does not see.
How could that which is the ground of non-seeing be the seeing of the capacity to see?
If one can see the ground of non-seeing, how could it not be you? Therefore, the Master Juefan said:
The World-Honored One has revealed the characteristics of seeing and not-seeing; one should immediately realize the true nature and need no longer seek through discrimination.
Furthermore, when you now see an object, since you see the object, the object also sees you.
Their essential natures are confused and entangled, yet they do not realize that the World-Honored One’s secret words for merging the mind clarify the enlightened mind through this very confusion.
Furthermore, it is said: "If you see at the moment of seeing, since the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, who else could it be but you?
Formerly, Zhao Jianzi had a minister named Zhou She, who stood at his gate for three days. Jianzi sent someone to question him, and he replied: "I wish—"
He was a remonstrating minister who used his pen and brush to record the ruler’s transgressions on tablets.
Whenever Jianzi stayed indoors, he stayed with him; whenever he went out, he went out with him. Before long, Zhou She died.
Later, while drinking at the Hongbo Terrace with his high officials, Jianzi wept as the wine flowed freely. All the officials fled, saying: "I am your subject..."
"There are those who commit offenses yet do not realize it themselves. Jianzi said, "The high officials are all without fault.
In the past, Shang Zhou fell silently while King Wu flourished through frankness. Now that Zhou She is dead, I have never heard of my own transgressions;
my downfall will come before long. This is why I weep."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing must be me and nothing else, [then it is as you say].
Yet these functions of the mind each have their respective locations; the branches of the applied dharma distinguish body and mind as separate.
Ānanda doubts that if the substance of seeing can indeed be all-pervasive, how could the substance of space expand and contract? And why does it cause [the vision] to be severed when obstructed?"
The World-Honored One said: "All sensory objects each belong to their respective external realms; thus, vision appears to expand or contract. Yet the substance of space has no fixed nature.
This indeterminate space can appear square or round, manifesting according to its vessel. However, if one merely removes the vessel's shape, the substance of space itself remains without shape."
One need not further eliminate the spatial characteristics of empty space. All sentient beings are deluded, taking themselves to be objects.
If one could instead transform objects, who would there be? The *I Ching* says: "The many dragons have no head; auspicious.
Duke Wen of Jin, while chasing a deer, lost it. He asked an old farmer, Lao Gu, saying, "Where is my deer? Lao Gu pointed with his foot and said: [The deer is here].
He departed accordingly. The Duke said, "I asked you about the toes; what was that? Lao Gu shook out his robes and rose, saying, "I did not expect a ruler to be like this.
Tigers and leopards dwell in seclusion, yet they become prey when they draw near to humans;
fish and turtles dwell in the deep, yet they are caught when they come to the shallows; the feudal lords suffer from their own crowds."
Consequently, his state was lost. Upon returning, Duke Wen was apprehensive; he encountered Luan Wuzi, who asked, "Did you catch any game on the hunt? Duke Wen had a look of joy on his face.

Luan Wuzi said, "I see that Your Majesty has lost something, yet you have a look of joy; what is the reason for this? Duke Wen replied, "I have lost something, but because I have obtained some excellent words, I have a look of joy.
Luan Wuzi asked, "Where is that man? Duke Wen said, "I did not come with him. Luan Wuzi said, "One who occupies a high position..."
He shows no compassion for those below him, yet he is arrogant; he is lax with commands but swift in punishment, yet he is tyrannical;
he takes others' words but rejects their persons, yet he is a thief. Duke Wen said, "Return and load up the ancient texts; let us go back together."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature... [until] ...to develop and awaken those who have not yet awakened.
Ānanda analyzed the subtle and profound workings of the faculties and distinguished the wondrous functions of body and mind.
Since the essence of vision is not my substance, what then are the body and mind? At this very moment, the body and mind possess substantiality through their discernment; as for that vision—
In truth, there is no discrimination. Why, then, do you say that "objects can see me"? Since seeing is not the mind, what then are the body and mind?
Below, I shall clarify the nature of the body and mind.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have just said—that the vision is right before you—is like the Tathāgata playing with so many snares to delude the people of the world and kill them with doubt.
It is a scene enacted within the play of words, a universe sketched upon the tongue; it fuses the present with the past, kicking the sea and striking the void."
Revealing the hand and eye within the shadowless, one extracts the essential clarity from amidst the myriad phenomena.
Wherever the hand points and wherever the mouth speaks, seeing is non-seeing as the mind merges; even a tree is non-tree as it manifests to the vision.
Is this present darkness the forest? Is clarity the sun? Is obstruction the wall? Is penetration empty space? Is it the refined brilliance extracted from among the myriad phenomena?
Or is it the refined vision carved out from the tip of the finger? Is it the source of the essence of seeing? As the ancient masters said:
"The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs; the stone tiger before the cliff embraces the void."
The child sleeps; the iron snake drills into the diamond eye. A Kunlun man rides an elephant while a heron leads the way. Gao Feng said:
"Within this there is one phrase that can grant and can take away, can kill and can bring to life.
If there is someone who can examine it through and through, the task of a lifetime of study will be finished. Right now, the dark is the forest, the light is the sun, and the obstruction is the wall.
"Penetration" is emptiness. Within it lies a single phrase that can release and enliven, and can also kill and seize.
If a person can discern this through investigation, I grant them the possession of one eye. Juefan said: "One may infer from this meaning."

The daily activities of all sentient beings are, in their ultimate essence, equal to perfect awakening. Within this state, there is not even a hair’s breadth of that which acts as a condition or an object of opposition.
Since conditions and oppositions cannot be found at all, from where could birth and death possibly arise?

What is called "speaking the truth" means that the five types of speech—whether true or false—are simply one and the same as suchness. The World-Honored One has often said that it is like a great mass of fire.
This is why it is so. The Dharma-gift of the World-Honored One may be called priceless. Having spoken cryptically, he speaks again with direct words:
"If the tree is seen, what further tree is there?"—this is the cryptic statement.
Within his own abiding samādhi, "seeing and the conditions for seeing"—this is the direct statement. If one savors these deeply and contemplates them minutely, both...
They are one and the same in cessation. How is this known? Because the tree is seen to be indivisible.
The World-Honored One intended for Ānanda to realize and clarify this for himself. However, even the observation of Master Juefan only explains one side;
he has not yet fully elucidated the purport within the sūtra. This body and mind function together. Have you not seen it in the sūtra text: "You may [move] subtly"?
"Peel away the myriad phenomena to extract the refined brilliance; reveal the source of pure and wondrous vision and point it out to me.
He further said, "That which is pointed to by a raised hand and that which is observed by a casting glance—these, together with true vision, mutually manifest enlightenment.
Now, analyze this minutely: what is it that extracts the refined brilliance? What is it that carves out the refined vision? And what is it that is pointed to by the raised hand?"
It must not be confused; it must not be bifurcated. It is the functioning of the whole body, yet there remains the doubt of perceiving it as divided objects.
Though one extracts its brilliant essence, this constitutes a distinction between substance and function. This is the quintessence of the One Vehicle; this chapter is even more extraordinary.

Its transformations are inexhaustible, its spiritual subtlety unfathomable, and its refinement profound and mysterious—like Sun Wu’s employment of troops, where killing and bringing to life depend entirely on himself.
With hands and eyes that turn heaven and earth with unimpeded mastery across both vertical and horizontal dimensions, and a pivotal mechanism unfathomable even to ghosts and spirits,
his divine spirit shines brilliantly, encompassing all true delight.

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, [spoke] from within the great multitude...

[regarding] what is right and what is not right. Milk within water is difficult to distinguish; the mind within words is difficult to discern. Mañjuśrī said: "The great assembly does not realize that the Tathāgata has elucidated the two kinds of refined vision:

What was it originally? In the midst of this, there is neither "is" nor "is not.
The World-Honored One has set out all these snares; he has utterly failed. Yet Mañjuśrī has seen through his leakage and identified the root source.
When the World-Honored One was questioned, he was like a mouse entering a cow’s horn—there was no place to turn. He truly revealed his inner state to Mañjuśrī.
Before your very eyes are the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, abiding within their own samādhi.
If these are taken together with the conceptualized appearances, they are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.

The thousand living words of the visible Tathāgata are all but the sounding of voices; they exhaustively pour forth from the liver and entrails, fusing and penetrating the single mind. Like wind startling the mist, it rises up.
Racing and wandering without ceasing—the burden carried by a fragrant elephant is not something a donkey can endure. Therefore, when crows cry and magpies screech, all recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;
when the pine waves roar and the valley echoes, they divide the mind and divide the vision. To realize that seeing returns to the mind—by then, the sword has long since departed.

Seeking to find the mind that seeks—this is like a hawk from Silla passing overhead. Had it not been for Mañjuśrī’s inspection, one would have been deluded by Śākyamuni the Old Man until future kalpas;
what end could there ever be to such a state? When he spoke to this point, he could not help but burst into laughter.
Those who embrace jade shoulder to shoulder; those who grasp pearls follow one after another.
“Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: apart from you, Mañjuśrī, is there another Mañjuśrī who is truly Mañjuśrī? Is it that there is no Mañjuśrī?
[This continues] until he says: “Pointing out what is not pointing.”
Do you still recognize this question of the World-Honored One? Where does it land? It leaves the whole world in doubt.
"If there were another Mañjuśrī like you, would that one be Mañjuśrī or not? Mañjuśrī replied, "So it is, World-Honored One.
